issues.legal_issue: A defendant may be transposed as an appellant when its participation in that capacity is needed to resolve the questions in the appeal completely and effectively.
material_facts: The State had been impleaded as a pro forma respondent in appeals brought by the acquiring authority.
The State and the authority raised the same challenge to the claimant’s entitlement to compensation.
The State had already disputed the claimant’s entitlement in the reference proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to transpose the State from respondent to appellant in order to adjudicate the dispute completely.
issues.legal_principle: Order I Rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers a court to add or rearrange parties whose presence is necessary for complete adjudication, and permits a defendant to be transposed to the category of plaintiff. The power may be exercised by an appellate court, including suo motu, in the interests of justice. The Court relied on Bhupendra Narayan Sinha v. Rajeshwar Prosad, AIR 1931 PC 162.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and party_already_before_court and party_has_same_interest_as_appellant and party_presence_needed_for_complete_adjudication

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is an appeal in which the court must resolve disputed issues between the parties.
predicates.party_already_before_court: The party whose status is changed is already before the court in another capacity.
predicates.party_has_same_interest_as_appellant: The party seeks the same outcome on the relevant issue as an existing appellant.
predicates.party_presence_needed_for_complete_adjud: The party’s participation as an appellant is needed to resolve all relevant questions effectively and completely.

issues.definition: When an appeal is pending, a party already before the court may be made an appellant if that party shares an appellant’s interest and its participation is needed for complete adjudication.

issues.legal_issue: An unappealed determination in one compensation reference does not bar review of entitlement where an appeal from a separate reference places that entitlement in issue.
material_facts: Separate references arising from the acquisition were decided by separate orders on the same day.
One reference involved the State’s claim to the compensation and the claimant’s claim to receive it.
An appeal was filed against the decision in another reference, in which the claimant’s entitlement to the compensation was also in issue.
The appellate challenge therefore put the entitlement question before the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not barred by res judicata from examining the claimant’s entitlement to the compensation in the appeal before it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure bars trial of a matter directly and substantially in issue that was directly and substantially in issue between the same parties litigating under the same title in a former proceeding and was heard and finally decided by a competent court. A finding that has attained finality may operate as res judicata. Badri Narayan Singh v. Kamdeo Prasad Singh, 1962 (3) SCR 759, and Premier Tyres Ltd. v. Kerala Road Transport Corporation, 1993 Supp (2) SCC 146, were distinguished because the challenged entitlement finding in this case was itself in an appealed reference.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is an appeal from a decision in a compensation reference.
predicates.separate_references_decided_separately: Related compensation questions were decided in separate reference proceedings rather than in a single consolidated proceeding.
predicates.entitlement_at_issue_in_appealed_referen: The claimant’s right to receive the compensation was contested in the reference whose decision was appealed.
predicates.entitlement_finding_not_final_in_that_re: The entitlement finding challenged on appeal had not become final in the reference under appeal.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a reference where entitlement remains contested, a separately decided reference does not bar review if the entitlement finding in the appealed reference is not final.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation court determines market value afresh on the evidence, and an appellate court need not disturb a valuation it considers high when the lower appellate court has affirmed it.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a sale of nearby land at a stated rate, a circle-rate certificate for the acquired locality, and a prior compensation decision for land in the area.
The claimant also relied on evidence about the flats constructed on the acquired land and their sale prices.
The reference court fixed the land value at Rs. 500 per square yard, and the High Court affirmed that valuation.
The acquired land was some distance from the more valuable locality used in one of the sale comparisons, and the Supreme Court considered the valuation apparently high.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not interfere with the land valuation affirmed by the High Court, notwithstanding its view that the market value appeared to have been fixed at a high figure.
issues.legal_principle: The Collector’s award is an offer, and the claimant bears the burden of proving that it is inadequate. A reference is treated as an original proceeding in which market value is determined afresh from the evidence produced. The Court relied on Chimanlal Hargovind Das v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, AIR 1988 SC 1652, and Periyar Pareekanni Rubbers v. State of Kerala, AIR 1990 SC 2192.

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and compensation_valuation_challenged and claimant_produced_market_value_evidence and high_court_affirmed_reference_valuation

predicates.appeal_proceeding: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation determined for acquired property.
predicates.compensation_valuation_challenged: A party challenges the market value fixed for the acquired land.
predicates.claimant_produced_market_value_evidence: The claimant relied on evidence such as comparable transactions, locality rates, or evidence of development and sale value.
predicates.high_court_affirmed_reference_valuation: The High Court affirmed the reference court’s valuation of the land.

issues.definition: When market value is challenged in a compensation appeal, evidence was produced and the High Court affirmed the reference valuation, the affirmed valuation is not disturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A deduction for internal development may be made when acquired land is used for multi-storey residential development and space must be left for internal infrastructure and open areas.
material_facts: The acquired land was in a developed area with an approach road and power lines available.
The acquisition was for construction of multi-storey residential flats.
The development required portions of the land to be left for internal roads, sewer lines, and open space.
The High Court deducted 20 per cent from the market value for internal development.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in deducting 20 per cent from the market value for internal development.
issues.legal_principle: A deduction of about one-third may normally be made when a large acquired area is not fully developed. The Court relied on Vijay Kumar Motilal v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1981 SC 1632; Sahib Singh Kalha v. Amritsar Improvement Trust, AIR 1982 SC 940; and Special Tehsildar Land Acquisition v. A. Mangla Gowri, AIR 1992 SC 666. The circumstances of the development and the land must be considered when fixing the deduction.

predicates.compensation_valuation_proceeding: The court is determining or reviewing compensation for acquired land.
predicates.land_acquired_for_multi_unit_development: The land is to be developed for multiple residential units.
predicates.internal_infrastructure_and_open_space_r: The development requires land to be reserved for internal infrastructure or open space.

issues.definition: A development deduction is justified in a compensation valuation when land acquired for multiple residential units must include internal infrastructure or open space.

issues.legal_issue: A claimed government decision to renew an expired lease must be established by reliable evidence of the government’s decision and cannot be proved merely through unexhibited photocopies of letters.
material_facts: The claimant relied on photocopies of two letters said to record a government decision to renew the lease.
The original letters were not produced, the copies were not exhibited, and they did not bear a government seal.
The claimant did not summon government records or a responsible government officer to prove that a renewal decision had been made.
The asserted renewal date and the timing of the acquisition raised further doubts about the letters.
issues.conclusion: The alleged government decision to renew the lease was not established by the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: A government decision to renew a lease must be proved through relevant government records produced by an appropriate authority or officer; the evidence offered here did not establish that such a decision had been made.

predicates.lease_renewal_claimed: A claimant asserts that a lease was renewed after its stated term expired.
predicates.renewal_claim_depends_on_government_deci: The asserted renewal depends on a decision said to have been made by the government.
predicates.no_reliable_government_records_or_offici: The claimant does not produce reliable government records or official testimony proving the asserted decision.

issues.definition: When a claimed lease renewal depends on a government decision that is not proved by reliable records or official evidence, the renewal is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A short-term lessee whose lease has expired or is about to expire is entitled only to compensation for the limited leasehold interest, while the reversionary owner is entitled to the remaining compensation.
material_facts: The acquired property was government land held under a lease, not land owned outright by the claimant.
The Court found that the lease had expired before possession was taken and that no renewal had been proved.
Even on the claimant’s account, possession was taken shortly before the asserted expiry of the lease.
The High Court apportioned the compensation equally between the claimant and the State.
issues.conclusion: The claimant was entitled to 20 per cent of the compensation for the land and the State was entitled to the remaining 80 per cent.
issues.legal_principle: A lessee’s limited interest is distinct from ownership and does not entitle the lessee to the entire compensation. Under Sections 105, 108, and 111(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, a lease transfers a right to enjoy property for a term and ordinarily determines by efflux of time. Compensation must reflect the interests acquired. The Court relied on Radha Charan v. Secretary of State, AIR 1943 Allahabad 238; Inder Parshad v. Union of India, 1994 (5) SCC 239; and Ratan Kumar Tandon v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1996 SC 2710, distinguishing the circumstances of a perpetual lease and the earlier acquisition made well before expiry.

rule.if: compulsory_acquisition_proceeding and claimant_holds_limited_leasehold_interest and lease_expired_or_near_expiry_at_possession and renewal_not_established

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for property acquired compulsorily.
predicates.claimant_holds_limited_leasehold_interes: The claimant holds a leasehold interest rather than ownership of the land.
predicates.lease_expired_or_near_expiry_at_possessi: The lease had expired or was due to expire shortly when possession was taken.
predicates.renewal_not_established: The claimant has not established that the lease was renewed.

issues.definition: When acquired property is held under a limited lease that has expired or is close to expiry and renewal is unproved, the lessee receives only a small share of the compensation.

issues.legal_issue: The value of a building is not reliably assessed by including the underlying land’s value again or by treating renovation as proof that the building’s original structure was renewed.
material_facts: The claimant’s consulting engineer included the land beneath the building when assessing the building’s value, although the land was separately valued.
The engineer assessed the building’s age from the date of renovation.
There was no evidence that the foundation, walls, and roof had been rebuilt during the renovation.
The High Court valued the building, which was more than 90 years old, at Rs. 60,000; it also assessed the trees at Rs. 23,000.
The Supreme Court found no ground to interfere with the High Court’s assessments of the building or the trees.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s valuation of the building at Rs. 60,000 and the trees at Rs. 23,000 was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Land and buildings ordinarily form one unit for valuation, and the composite value should generally be determined by comparable properties or income from the property rather than by simply adding separate values. Separate assessment may be permissible where extensive land has development potential not reflected in the structures; a building may be assessed by construction or replacement cost less depreciation. The Court relied on Abdullah Jan Mohammad Ganjee v. State of Bihar, 1967 (1) SCWR 214; State of Kerala v. P.P. Hassan Koya, AIR 1968 SC 1201; O. Janardhan Reddy v. Special Deputy Collector, 1994 (6) SCC 456; State of Bihar v. Madheshwar Prasad, 1996 (6) SCC 197; State of Bihar v. Ratanlal Sahu, 1996 (10) SCC 635; and Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector, Varanasi, AIR 1988 SC 943.

rule.if: compensation_valuation_appeal and building_and_land_separately_assessed and building_assessment_includes_land_value_again or compensation_valuation_appeal and building_age_based_on_renovation_without_proof_of_structural_rebuilding

predicates.compensation_valuation_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired property.
predicates.building_and_land_separately_assessed: The land and a building on it are assessed as separate components.
predicates.building_assessment_includes_land_value_: The building valuation includes the value of land that has already been valued separately.
predicates.building_age_based_on_renovation_without: The building’s age is assessed from renovation even though there is no evidence that its principal structure was rebuilt.

issues.definition: In a compensation valuation appeal, an assessment that double-counts land or treats renovation as structural rebuilding is faulty and does not displace a supported lower-court valuation.

issues.legal_issue: An award of costs to a party that successfully appeals and obtains modification of the compensation award is justified.
material_facts: The acquiring authority appealed against the reference court’s award.
The High Court accepted the authority’s appeal in part and modified the award.
The High Court directed that costs be paid to the authority.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s direction awarding costs to the acquiring authority was justified.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that, where the High Court accepted the acquiring authority’s appeal and modified the reference court’s award, its direction regarding costs was justified.

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party appeals from an award made in a compensation proceeding.
predicates.appealing_party_succeeds_in_obtaining_aw: The appealing party obtains a modification of the award.

issues.definition: When an appellant obtains a modification of a compensation award, a costs award in its favor is justified.
